title: Managing Family Income
summary: Income is whatever comes into the family in the form of money – salary, part-time earnings, rent from a house or shop, bank interest, profit from shares and investments, earnings from skills or household produce. Using skills (stitching, kitchen garden, knitting) saves money that would have been paid out and adds to income; free facilities (medical, free education, rent-free accommodation) also save money. Family income is the income from all sources like salary of family members, rents, bank interest and savings from the use of family members' skills. Expenditure is the money spent from the income to meet needs – food, housing, clothing, education, transport, medical expenses, entertainment and others. Saving is the money set aside by the family for use in times of need (emergencies, children's education or marriage, old age, health).
## Managing income and the spending plan

If expenditure is more than income the family has to borrow; if expenditure is less than income the family saves. Managing income means planning expenditure so that all needs are met within the income; the tool is a spending plan or budget – a list of requirements of family members with the money allocated to each, based on the total income. Steps: (1) keep in mind all income and facilities available for the period; (2) list all requirements; (3) prioritise the needs; (4) allocate funds keeping the total income in mind; (5) balance the plan; then keep records of all expenditure. Records help to know how much was spent on each item, control unnecessary expenditure, plan for the future, save money, compare prices and avoid being cheated.

Allocation depends on: income of the family; size of family (more members – more on food and clothing, less on entertainment); age of members (school-going children – education); place of residence (cost of living is higher in big cities); skills of members (fewer repair bills); and savings for the future. A guide table for an income of Rs 10,000 is: food 35% (Rs 3,500), housing 20% (Rs 2,000), clothing 5% (Rs 500), recreation 5% (Rs 500), household operations 6% (Rs 600), education 5% (Rs 500), transport 8% (Rs 800), medical 3% (Rs 300), furnishing 3% (Rs 300), savings 10% (Rs 1,000). It is advisable to save about 10% of the monthly income.

Balancing is making expenditure less than income, in two ways: earn more (tuitions, stitching, handicrafts, part-time job or overtime, kitchen garden, poultry, bee-keeping, making preserved foods) or cut expenditure (no food waste, less eating out, watch electricity and water use, iron and wash at home, economical use of stationery, public transport or cycle, public library, look for sales and rebates, shop in one trip, avoid impulsive buying, fund unnecessary items last). A spending plan discourages impulsive buying and helps meet all needs.

Accurate estimate of income (gross income differs from take-home pay); accurate estimate of expenditure (use past records); reasonably accurate allocation of money (anticipate festivals, etc.); and flexibility (a margin so that money can be diverted, for example from entertainment to an unexpected medical expense). A budget helps in living within income, achieving long-term goals, setting priorities and saving.

objective: State True or False: (i) Funds should be allocated keeping in mind total income. (ii) Family income includes money from salary, rent and bank interest only. (iii) Cost of living is more in big cities. (iv) Expenditure should be less than income to save.

State True or False: (i) A budget is the process of allocating income among various uses. (ii) A budget cannot help in achieving long-term goals. (iii) Income of family members does not influence the budget. (iv) The main purpose of a budget is to live within income.
(i) True. (ii) False – it can help. (iii) False – it does. (iv) True.

sa: Mr Gupta lives in his own house with his children aged 17 and 20 years. He earns Rs 38,000 a month. Prepare a spending plan for his family.

Using the guide percentages on Rs 38,000: food 35% = 38,000 x 35/100 = Rs 13,300; housing (repairs, taxes, utilities) 20% = Rs 7,600; clothing 5% = Rs 1,900; recreation 5% = Rs 1,900; household operations 6% = Rs 2,280; education 5% = Rs 1,900; transport 8% = Rs 3,040; medical 3% = Rs 1,140; furnishing 3% = Rs 1,140; savings 10% = Rs 3,800. Total = 13,300 + 7,600 + 1,900 + 1,900 + 2,280 + 1,900 + 3,040 + 1,140 + 1,140 + 3,800 = Rs 38,000, so the plan is balanced. (Education may be raised a little by trimming recreation.)
Prepare a spending plan for a family with a monthly income of Rs 31,000 using the guide percentages.

Food 35% = Rs 10,850; housing 20% = Rs 6,200; clothing 5% = Rs 1,550; recreation 5% = Rs 1,550; household operations 6% = Rs 1,860; education 5% = Rs 1,550; transport 8% = Rs 2,480; medical 3% = Rs 930; furnishing 3% = Rs 930; savings 10% = Rs 3,100. Total = 10,850 + 6,200 + 1,550 + 1,550 + 1,860 + 1,550 + 2,480 + 930 + 930 + 3,100 = Rs 31,000.
Sonali cannot meet her monthly expenses with her present income. Suggest ways to balance her spending plan.

She can earn more (tuitions, stitching, handicrafts, a part-time job, kitchen garden or preserved foods) or cut down expenses (avoid food waste and eating out, save electricity and water, use public transport, iron and wash at home, use the public library, buy during sales, avoid impulsive buying, and allot funds to unnecessary items last).
List the characteristics of a good budget.

It has accurate estimates of income (gross income differs from take-home pay); accurate estimates of expenditure based on past records; reasonably accurate allocation that anticipates festivals and future changes; and it is flexible, with a margin so money can be moved from one item to another.
la: Explain the steps of making a spending plan and the factors on which allocation of money to different items depends.

Steps: keep in mind all income and facilities; list all requirements; prioritise needs; allocate funds according to total income; balance the plan (earn more or cut expenses) and keep records. Allocation depends on income of the family, size of the family, age of family members (school-going children), place of residence (cost of living is higher in big cities), skills of members and the amount to be saved (about 10%).
Write five points highlighting the importance of a family spending plan.

(1) It helps the family live within its income. (2) It helps to save money for future needs and emergencies. (3) It avoids borrowing. (4) It discourages impulsive buying. (5) It helps to meet all needs of all family members by listing and prioritising them. (6) Records help to control unnecessary expenses and avoid being cheated.
